newsitem.title: DUBAI: Ekeus says Iraq obstructs U.N. arms inspectors.
newsitem.headline: Ekeus says Iraq obstructs U.N. arms inspectors.

text.p: The United Nations official in charge of destroying Iraq's deadliest weapons said in remarks published on Friday that Baghdad has obstructed U.N. efforts to study parts of Scud missiles.

"(Deputy Prime Minister) Tareq Aziz blocked our team as they were trying to transport the missile parts to our centre in Baghdad after digging them out of the ground," Rolf Ekeus told the United Arab Emirates English-language daily The Gulf Today of the November 15 incident.
"What followed was a rather unpleasant exchange," added Ekeus, who is due to arrive in Kuwait on Friday as part of a Gulf tour.
A senior U.N. official said this week that the U.N. planned to take the remains of missiles for study outside Iraq to help assess Baghdad's claims that all Scuds have been destroyed.
In 1992 Iraq gave the U.N. a list of hundreds of missiles, launch vehicles and other weapons it said it had destroyed and buried in July 1991.
Terms of the ceasefire that ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait ban Iraq from having missiles with a range greater than 150 km (94 miles) and the means to produce them.
Ekeus has said Iraq was still concealing as many as 16 missiles.

Ekeus said he had written a letter to Aziz, saying that Iraq violated U.N. Security Council Resolution 687 which calls on it to yield possession of any mass destruction weapons for removal, the newspaper said.
A copy of the letter was also sent to the U.N. Security Council, said Ekeus, chief of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) overseeing the elimination of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, .
"As a result the UNSCOM removal team left Iraq. But before they left, they were jostled by security men who tried to search their cargo...," Ekeus told The Gulf Today.

Aziz replied to Ekeus' letter, saying that the removal of Scuds was "not the type of joint work" envisaged by the joint action programme which was agreed by him and Ekeus at a meeting in last June, the newspaper reported.
Ekeus recently said he would try a new tack with Iraqi political leaders on his mission next month in an effort to press Iraq to disclose information on unaccounted for ballistic missiles.
